slides.h: Eleven native herbs. Here is the first.
slides.b: Kia ora. This summer we are teaching what helps when something hurts, one native herb a week. We start with harakeke.
Summer is when the injuries happen. We will share what to do in the first 48 hours, how to use what you have, and when to see your GP.
Relief for everyday aches and bumps. Joints for stiffness and mobility. Sports for warm-up and recovery. The eleven herbs are spread across the three.
New Zealand flax. You know it from riverbanks, wetlands and back fences all over Aotearoa. Its gel has long been valued in rongoā rākau, Māori plant medicine.

posts.caption:

posts.title: Rub it in, not on
posts.about: How-to Reel showing why massage matters as much as the herbs, so people use the product properly and get more from it.
posts.headline: Rub it in, not just on
posts.subline: Twenty seconds of massage does half the work

shots.shot: Close on a hand dabbing rub onto a shoulder and stopping, the rub sitting on the skin
Same hand now pressing in slow circles with the fingertips, skin moving under them
shots.text: Rub it in, not just on

shots.shot: Thumb working along the top of the shoulder toward the neck, firm and slow
shots.text: Massage warms the area and helps the herbs absorb

shots.shot: Wider shot, person rolling the shoulder back, relaxed face
Lid going back on a Sports Rub jar on a wooden bench
End card: green ground, logo

posts.caption:
The massage matters as much as what is in the jar.

A dab of rub sitting on your skin does very little. Rub it in with slow, firm circles for a good 20 seconds. Massage warms the area, eases the tightness around the sore spot, and helps the herbs absorb.

Try it like this:
A small amount on your fingertips.
Slow circles, firm enough to move the skin.
Work outward from the sore spot.
Wash your hands after, and keep it away from your eyes.

If a pain is sharp, getting worse, or came from a fall or a big knock, see your GP before you start rubbing.

We filmed this with the Sports Rub, and the same goes for every rub in the range. Save this one for later.

posts.title: Three summer sport injuries
posts.about: Injury first-aid post on the three injuries that come back with summer sport, so people know what to do on the day.
posts.headline: Summer sport is back. So are these.
posts.subline: The three injuries we hear about most in November

steps.t: Rest, ice in short bursts, compress, raise it. Can't bear weight? See your GP.
Warm up properly, stretch after, ease back in. Week one is not a final.
Paddling and throwing load shoulders fast. Build up, rest when it aches.

posts.caption:
Touch, cricket and surf are back, and so are the same three injuries every November.

1. Rolled ankle. Rest it, ice in short bursts, a firm bandage, and keep it raised. If you can't put weight on it, or it is badly swollen or misshapen, see your GP. It may be more than a sprain.

2. Tight calves and hamstrings. The first few weeks are when they go. Warm up properly, stretch after, and build up slowly.

3. Sore shoulders. Paddling and throwing ask a lot of a shoulder that has had the winter off. Do less than you think for the first fortnight.

After the first 48 hours, a rub massaged in can support tired muscles while you get moving again. The Sports range is made for that job.

posts.caption:
A good summer first-aid kit lives where the injuries happen: the bach, the car and the sports bag.

Here is what goes in ours.
For cuts and blisters: plasters, blister pads, strapping tape, antiseptic wipes and tweezers.
For sprains and knocks: a crepe bandage, an instant ice pack, and the number for the nearest medical centre written down. Phone signal at the bach is not a given.
For the days after: a rub for tired muscles, bumps and bruises. Relief for the family, Sports for the ones who overdo it. Roll-ons fit a glovebox.

If a knock is serious, the kit is not the answer. See your GP or call 111.

posts.caption:
Horopito is the native pepper tree, and the name tells you why: bite a leaf and it bites back.

It is a small shrub with red-blotched leaves that grows in our forests from the North Island hills down to Stewart Island. In rongoā rākau, Māori plant medicine, horopito was traditionally used for the skin and for circulation. That warming quality is what drew us to it.

Today it sits in our {RANGE} range, working alongside other native herbs. No single herb does the job on its own, which is why each of our jars holds 11 to 14 active ingredients, where most rubs use 5 or 6.

posts.title: How much to use: knee demo
posts.about: How-to Reel answering the FAQ on how much to use and when, filmed on a knee after a shower.
posts.headline: How much rub? Less than you think
posts.subline: 1 to 5 ml, after a shower, rubbed in

shots.shot: Steam-fogged bathroom mirror, towel over a shoulder, a knee bent on the edge of the bath
shots.text: After a shower is the best time

shots.shot: Fingertip scooping a pea-sized amount from the jar
Slow circles around and above the knee, skin moving
shots.text: Warm skin, open pores. Massage it in

shots.shot: Knee straightening and bending slowly
shots.text: Up to five times a day

shots.shot: End card: green ground, logo

posts.caption:
How much rub should you use? Less than most people think: 1 to 5 ml, about a fingertip to a teaspoon.

Timing helps too. Apply it when the pores are open, after a warm shower or straight after training. Then massage it in properly with slow circles until it has gone.

You can use it up to five times a day.

New to it? Patch test first. Try a small amount on the inside of your wrist and wait 24 hours before using it more widely. Keep it away from eyes and broken skin, and wash your hands after.

If a knee is swollen, hot, locking or giving way, see your GP before you treat it yourself.

Save this for the next time you open a jar.

posts.title: Your bruise colour is a clock
posts.about: Injury first-aid post explaining what each bruise colour means and when a bruise needs a doctor.
posts.headline: What is your bruise telling you?
posts.subline: The colour is a clock

steps.t: Day one or two. Fresh blood under the skin. Cold pack, rest, raise it.
Days three to six. Your body is breaking it down. Gentle warmth helps.
About a week on. Nearly done. It should fade within two weeks.

posts.caption:
A bruise changes colour as it heals, so the colour tells you roughly how old it is.

Red to purple: day one or two. Fresh blood has pooled under the skin. A cold pack in short bursts, rest and raising it help in the first 48 hours.

Blue to green: days three to six. Your body is breaking the blood down. Gentle warmth and light massage around, not on, a sore spot can help.

Yellow to brown: about a week in. Nearly there. Most bruises fade within two weeks.

See your GP if a bruise appears for no reason, is very large or swollen, sits over a joint you can't move, or isn't fading after two weeks.

Our Relief range is the one we keep for bumps and bruises. Save this for the next knock.

posts.caption:
The question we get most: which one should I buy? Two steps.

Step one: the range.
Relief is mid strength, for everyday aches, bumps, bruises, sprains and growing pains. Suitable from age five.
Joints is higher strength, for stiffness and mobility when joint pain is long-term. Rub only.
Sports is higher strength, for warm-up and recovery when you are active, or when pain is long-standing.

Step two: the format.
Rub: a cocoa butter base. Best for massaging in.
Spray: an alcohol base. Quick, no hands needed, good at the sideline.
Roll-on: both bases. Small, no mess, made for bags and gloveboxes.

Still not sure? Comment below with what hurts and we will point you in the right direction. We are pinning this one.

posts.caption:
We get asked this a lot, so Jess answers it herself.

We have been friends since we met at primary school in West Auckland, aged six, with the Waitākere Ranges on our doorstep. After years in corporate jobs, Jess in commercial real estate and Dan in advertising, we wanted to do something more meaningful.

So we bought a small business from a horse trainer. She had made a rub for her race horses' tight, sore muscles, and when friends and family kept asking for "that horse stuff", she made one for people. We did a rongoā course, did our research, and reformulated it. The original had two native herbs, harakeke and kūmarahou. Today there are eleven, across three ranges.

That is still the whole idea. Move freely, live naturally.

Got a question for Jess or Dan? Ask it in the comments and we may answer it on camera.

Ngā mihi, Jess and Dan

slides.h: Five things in a tramper's first-aid kit
slides.b: Peak tramping season is here. This is what lives in our packs. Number four is a roll-on.
Blister plasters, strapping tape and small scissors. Treat a hot spot the moment you feel it, not at the hut.
For a rolled ankle or a sore knee on a long descent. Light, cheap and it does a lot.
Weighs almost nothing. Weather turns fast in the hills, even in December.

posts.caption:
Five things in a tramper's first-aid kit, and number four is a roll-on.

1. Blister care: plasters, strapping tape and small scissors. Treat hot spots early.
2. A crepe bandage for a rolled ankle or a sore knee on the way down.
3. A survival blanket. December weather in the hills still turns.
4. A roll-on for tight calves and sore feet at the end of the day. Our Sports roll-on fits the lid pocket.
5. A plan someone else knows. Leave your intentions at home and carry a locator beacon on remote tracks.

And know when to turn back. If someone can't bear weight, has knocked their head, or is cold and confused, stop and get help.

posts.title: Herb three: Kūmarahou, gumdiggers' soap
posts.about: Herb-of-the-week Reel filmed in the bush on kūmarahou, the gumdiggers' soap, and which ranges it is in.
posts.headline: Kūmarahou, the gumdiggers' soap
posts.subline: Herb three of eleven, in the bush

shots.shot: Kūmarahou shrub on a clay bank in the bush, slow push in
Close on the pale yellow flower heads
Wet hands rubbing flowers together, a light lather forming
shots.text: Crush the flowers with water and they lather

shots.shot: Jars of Joints Rub and Sports Rub on a mossy log
shots.text: In our Joints and Sports ranges

shots.shot: End card: green ground, logo

posts.caption:
Kūmarahou is known as gumdiggers' soap. Crush the flowers with a little water and they lather in your hands, which is how the old gumdiggers washed up in the north.

It is a native shrub that grows on poor clay soils, mostly in the upper North Island, and it flowers pale yellow in spring. In rongoā rākau, Māori plant medicine, kūmarahou has a long history of traditional use.

It is herb three in our series, and you will find it in our Joints and Sports ranges.

We filmed this one in the bush. Have you seen kūmarahou flowering? Tell us where in the comments.

posts.title: Day two on the track
posts.about: Injury first-aid post on the three things that go wrong on day two of a tramp: hot spots, blisters and tight calves.
posts.headline: Day two on the track
posts.subline: Hot spots, blisters and tight calves

steps.t: Stop now. Dry the skin and tape over it before it becomes a blister.
If it is intact, leave it whole. Cover with a blister plaster.
Stretch at every break. Massage them at the hut that night.

posts.caption:
Day two is when the track catches up with you.

Hot spot: that warm rub on your heel or toe. Stop as soon as you feel it. Dry the skin, tape over it, and check your sock is not bunched. Five minutes now saves three days of limping.

Blister: if it is intact, leave it whole. The skin over it is the best dressing you have. Cover it with a blister plaster. If it has burst, clean it and cover it.

Tight calves: day one's climbs show up on day two. Stretch at every break, and at the hut massage them properly. A rub worked in that night can support tired muscles before tomorrow.

See your GP if a blister shows redness spreading, swelling, pus or heat. Those are signs of infection.

Save this for your next multi-day.

posts.title: Three stretches before touch
posts.about: Wellness Reel with a 90-second pre-touch warm-up in three moves, no product in shot, to earn saves and reach.
posts.headline: Three stretches before touch
posts.subline: Ninety seconds. Do them every game

shots.shot: Touch players arriving at a field in the evening, boots going on
Player doing leg swings, front to back, holding a fence
Walking lunges with a twist over the front knee
Calf raises on the sideline, then quick ankle circles
Team running out onto the field, end card with logo

posts.caption:
Ninety seconds before touch can save you six weeks on the sideline.

1. Leg swings. Hold a fence or a mate, swing each leg front to back 10 times. Loosens the hamstrings and hips.

2. Walking lunge with a twist. Ten steps, turning your chest over the front knee. Wakes up the hips, quads and back.

3. Calf raises, then ankle circles. Fifteen raises, then circle each ankle both ways. Calves and ankles take the most load in touch.

Move into each one, don't bounce, and keep it gentle. Then a couple of easy jogs before the first sprint.

If something pulls sharp during a game, stop. Playing on through a sharp pain is how small injuries get big.

posts.title: Bumps, bruises and grazes
posts.about: Parent-focused injury first-aid carousel: what is normal for bumps, bruises and grazes, what needs a doctor, with the Relief Rub as one step and the blog's when-to-get-help line last.
posts.headline: Bumps, bruises and grazes
posts.subline: What is normal, and what needs a doctor

slides.b: Summer holidays mean scraped knees and the odd egg on the forehead. Here is what is normal, and what needs a doctor.
Some swelling, colour changes over a week or two, sore to touch but they can still move it. A cold pack in the first 48 hours.
Clean it with water, take out any grit, cover it. It should look a little better each day.
Once the skin is unbroken, a gentle rub can help. Our Relief Rub is suitable from age five. Never on open grazes.
They can't bear weight, a limb looks misshapen, pain gets worse after 48 hours, or a graze shows spreading redness, heat or pus.
After a head knock: vomiting, drowsiness, confusion or a headache that gets worse. Call 111 or go to A and E.

slides.h: Rub it, rest it, or ring someone?
slides.b: Our blog on severe muscle pain has the honest line on when to get help. Link in bio.

posts.caption:
Summer holidays bring scraped knees and the odd bump on the head. Most are normal. A few need a doctor.

Normal: a bump or bruise with some swelling that changes colour over a week or two, and a graze that looks a little better each day. Cold pack in the first 48 hours. Clean grazes with water and cover them.

See your GP if they can't bear weight, a limb looks misshapen, pain gets worse after 48 hours, or a graze shows spreading redness, heat or pus.

After a head knock, watch for vomiting, drowsiness, confusion or a worsening headache. That is a 111 call or a trip to A and E.

For everyday bumps and bruises on unbroken skin, our Relief Rub is suitable from age five.

This week's blog is a parent's guide to bumps, bruises and growing pains. Link in bio. Save this one for the holidays.

posts.caption:
Everyone knows kōwhai for its yellow spring flowers and the tūī that feed on them. Fewer people know the rest of the tree.

Kōwhai grows along riverbanks and forest edges right across Aotearoa. In rongoā rākau, Māori plant medicine, {KOWHAI_USE}.

It is herb four in our series, and it lives in our Sports range, working alongside the other native herbs in that jar.

A safety note: kōwhai seeds are poisonous, so keep little ones from putting them in their mouths. Admire the tree, don't eat it.

posts.title: Growing pains are real
posts.about: Wellness post for parents: what doctors know about growing pains and what helps at bedtime, with clear signs to see a GP.
posts.headline: Growing pains are real
posts.subline: What helps at bedtime

steps.t: Slow strokes on the calves and thighs. It comforts as much as it soothes.
A warm bath or heat pack before bed can ease the ache.
Light calf and thigh stretches in the evening, especially after a busy day.

posts.caption:
Growing pains are real, and they are common.

Doctors describe them as an aching in both legs, usually the calves, thighs or behind the knees, that comes in the late afternoon or at night. They are most common in children aged about three to twelve, often after an active day, and they are gone by morning.

What helps at bedtime: gentle massage on the legs, a warm bath or heat pack, and some light stretches.

See your GP if the pain is in one leg only, is in a joint, is still there in the morning, or comes with swelling, redness, a limp or a fever. Those are not growing pains.

Our Relief range is suitable from age five, and massaging it in is part of the bedtime routine for a lot of families.

Save this for the next time a little one can't sleep.

posts.caption:
"Is it safe for kids?" It is one of the questions we get most, so Jess is answering it here, straight from the label.

Relief range: suitable from age five.
Joints and Sports ranges: from age seven. They are higher strength.
Not for use while pregnant or breastfeeding.

A few more things from Jess: patch test first on the inside of the wrist, keep it away from eyes and broken skin, and wash your hands after applying it to a child. If your child's pain is severe, keeps coming back, or came from a fall, see your GP first.

posts.caption:
The bach cupboard is where summer first aid actually happens. Stock it once and leave it there.

The first-aid tin: plasters, a crepe bandage, tweezers for splinters, antiseptic, and the local medical centre's number written inside the lid.

Sun and bugs: sunscreen, a spare hat, insect repellent and something for sunburn.

For bumps and aches: a Relief Rub for the family's bumps, bruises and sore backs from the long drive, and a roll-on for the beach bag. Relief is suitable from age five.

As Pearl from Auckland told us, "I can't live without it."

posts.title: Gardening recovery: wrists, back, knees
posts.about: Wellness Reel for gardeners, our core older customer: a 20-second recovery routine for wrists, lower back and knees after a session in the garden.
posts.headline: After the garden: 20 seconds
posts.subline: Wrists, lower back, knees

shots.shot: Gloved hands pulling weeds in a vege garden, then gloves coming off
Wrist circles, then gently pressing the palms together and down
shots.text: Wrists: circles, then a gentle stretch

shots.shot: Standing, hands on lower back, slow lean back
shots.text: Lower back: hands on hips, lean back slowly

shots.shot: Seated on the garden step, slow knee straightening, one leg at a time
Joints Rub worked into a knuckle and wrist; end card with logo

posts.caption:
Gardening season is here, and wrists, lower backs and knees feel it first.

A 20-second routine for when you down tools:
Wrists: ten slow circles each way, then press your palms together and lower them gently.
Lower back: stand tall, hands on your hips, and lean back slowly three times.
Knees: sit on the step and straighten each leg slowly, ten times.

Then, if your joints are stiff, massage in a little rub. Our Joints Rub is made for stiffness and mobility, and a lot of our customers keep a jar by the back door.

If a joint is hot, swollen or suddenly painful, or back pain runs down your leg, see your GP.

Save this, and send it to the gardener in your family.
